title: Lattice-quantile estimation of π and convex-region integrals from coined two-dimensional quantum walks
authors: Jen-Yu Chang, En-Jui Kuo, Chih-Yu Chen, Tsung-Wei Huang
abstract: Monte Carlo integration is fundamentally limited by the M^(-1/2) rate that the Cramer-Rao bound imposes on any sample-mean estimator of an expectation value, regardless of how the samples are drawn. Coined discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs) are known to spread ballistically - their position variance scales as T^2 against the diffusive T of classical random walks - yet this faster spreading has not been exploited for numerical integration. We show that coupling the ballistic scaling of a 2D DTQW to the Hardy-Huxley asymptotic for Gauss circle lattice counts produces estimators whose dominant error is a deterministic number-theoretic residual controlled by walk depth T, not a statistical fluctuation controlled by sample count M. The construction replaces the empirical mean of a sample-mean estimator with the ratio N(R-hat)/R-hat^2 of a lattice count to the square of a radial position quantile, a structural change that sidesteps the Cramer-Rao barrier. A single batch of measurements then propagates through classically precomputed multipliers to cover an entire family of integrals simultaneously. We develop the framework for convex smooth domains via Kraetzel's lattice asymptotic and for smooth integrals with convex or annular super-level sets via Cavalieri's principle, and provide a parameter-free identity for the bias floor (validated to within 1.5x across all tested depths). Every experiment is benchmarked against the classical random walk with the identical estimator to isolate the quantum contribution; the framework is oracle-free in the QAE sense (no controlled unitary encoding the integrand is required) and structurally distinct from quantum amplitude estimation and Szegedy-walk approaches. These ratios compare measurement counts at fixed precision and do not include quantum circuit execution cost.
summary: This work introduces a novel lattice-quantile estimator for integrals by leveraging the ballistic spread of 2D coined quantum walks. By replacing statistical averaging with ratios derived from lattice point counts, it bypasses the Cramér-Rao bound limitations faced by standard Monte Carlo methods. The technique allows for highly precise estimation of geometric constants and physical quantities like energy spectra using significantly fewer measurements than classical counterparts.
main_problem: To develop a numerical integration technique for estimating geometric quantities like $\pi$ and convex-region integrals that bypasses the fundamental statistical error scaling ($\mathcal{M}^{-1/2}$) of standard Monte Carlo methods.
main_result: The method achieves an error floor dominated by deterministic number-theoretic residuals controlled by walk depth $T$, leading to a superior convergence rate compared to classical random walks and uniform MC.
method: It replaces the empirical sample mean with a ratio estimator, $ rac{N(\hat{R})}{\hat{R}^2}$, derived from coupling the ballistic spreading of 2D quantum walks (DTQWs) to lattice point counting asymptotics (Hardy-Huxley).
model_or_system: The physical system is a coined discrete-time quantum walk on a 2D square lattice, analyzed using various coin operators (Grover, Hadamard, Fourier). The method applies to integrals whose super-level sets are convex or annular.
key_observables: Estimates for $\pi$, areas of convex regions, and energy level spacings ($\hbar\omega$) of the 2D harmonic oscillator.
important_parameters: Walk depth $T$ (controls ballistic spreading), sample count $M$, lattice counting exponent $\gamma$, and quantile parameter $\alpha$.
main_assumptions: The method is limited to integrals reducible to convex-region lattice counts; the analysis relies on asymptotic theorems like Hardy-Huxley and Krätzel's lattice asymptotics.
figures_summary: Figures compare the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) scaling of QW vs. RW/MC, showing the flat, lower bias floor for QW measurements; other figures illustrate the mechanism of oscillation in single-radius readouts versus phase-averaged results.
paper_structure: The paper develops the estimator by first establishing the lattice-quantile framework for $\pi$ (disk), then generalizing it to convex regions via Cavalieri's principle, and finally applying this structure to reconstruct entire families of integrals (e.g., harmonic oscillator energy levels) using a single measurement.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete demonstration of how quantum dynamics (ballistic spreading) can be harnessed in a non-algorithmic way—as a superior sampling resource—to solve fundamental problems in computational mathematics and physics, surpassing classical limits.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
